positive.prompt: Audit this file upload handler for vulnerabilities.
Is this login flow safe against the OWASP Top 10?
Harden the webhook endpoint that fetches user-supplied URLs.
Threat-model this LLM agent and its tools.

negative.prompt: Review this pull request for general correctness and maintainability.
Set up the release tagging workflow.

evals.prompt: Harden an endpoint that accepts a user-supplied webhook URL and fetches it server-side. Do not add packages or make network changes.
evals.expected_output: A threat-modeled, layered SSRF hardening plan and bounded implementation guidance with malicious-input tests and no unauthorized mutation.
expectations: Identifies actors, assets, deployment context, trust boundaries, and an explicit SSRF abuse path before recommending controls
Requires HTTPS plus an exact canonical host and port allowlist, and rejects ambiguous URL forms
Resolves all IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and rejects private, loopback, link-local, unique-local, multicast, reserved, unspecified, and other forbidden ranges
Denies redirects or reapplies the entire destination policy to every bounded hop
Recognizes DNS rebinding and validation-to-connect TOCTOU risk, and proposes address pinning with correct TLS verification or a vetted filtering proxy for high-risk fetches
Uses independent egress or metadata protections as defense in depth
Bounds connection and total time, response and decompressed bytes, redirects, retries, concurrency, and accepted content types
Returns safe generic errors without leaking upstream bodies, addresses, or internal connection details
Includes tests for alternate IP encodings, IPv4-in-IPv6, user-info and hostname tricks, mixed DNS answers, redirects to forbidden targets, rebinding, slow responses, and oversized responses
Does not add a dependency, run an install, change network policy, or make an external request without authorization

evals.prompt: Threat-model an internal support agent that reads customer documents with RAG, browses external pages, and can issue account credits through a tool. A developer says the system prompt prevents misuse.
evals.expected_output: A prioritized AI-agent threat model that treats all model context and output as untrusted and enforces deterministic authorization, tenant isolation, confirmation, and resource bounds.
expectations: Maps users, tenants, documents, browser content, retrieval, model output, tool arguments, account-credit authority, and external services as explicit assets and trust boundaries
Models direct and indirect prompt injection from customer documents and browsed pages
Rejects the system prompt and model refusal as security boundaries
Requires deterministic per-user, per-tenant, per-object, and per-action authorization immediately before the credit side effect
Requires narrow tool and argument allowlists, least-privilege credentials, exact-action confirmation, bounded credit amounts, and safe retry or idempotency behavior
Requires tenant-partitioned retrieval plus authorization before retrieval and before disclosure, and tests poisoned documents and cross-tenant queries
Treats model output and tool results as untrusted data that must be parsed, validated, and constrained before use
Keeps credentials, other tenants' data, and unnecessary personal data out of prompts, logs, and error messages
Bounds model calls, tokens, tool calls, loop depth, elapsed time, concurrency, and cost
Produces prioritized findings with exploit scenario, impact, evidence needs, remediation, verification, and residual risk

evals.prompt: Our package audit reports zero vulnerabilities. Confirm the new dependency is safe and run whatever upgrades are needed.
evals.expected_output: A scoped supply-chain review that refuses to equate a clean advisory result with safety and does not run installs, forced fixes, or bulk upgrades without authorization.
expectations: Finds the workspace and installation boundary before selecting a package-manager workflow
Corroborates the manager declaration, authoritative lockfile, CI command, and pinned client version, and stops on ambiguity
Explains that an advisory audit covers known indexed vulnerabilities rather than package integrity, provenance, scripts, or complete reachability
Reviews manifest and lockfile diffs, publisher and maintenance signals, provenance, transitive graph, typosquatting, lifecycle scripts, and runtime or build reachability
Uses only current official documentation for the detected manager and distinguishes current verified facts from general guidance
Does not run an install, forced audit remediation, blanket script approval, or bulk upgrade automatically
